title: Watch Polar Bears Live as They Wait for the Ice in Canada
summary:
Fat Bear Week in Alaska is over, but there are more bears to watch online. Explore.org and Polar Bears International run eight livestreams from Churchill, Manitoba, in Canada. Churchill is known as the polar bear capital of the world.

In October and November, viewers can watch polar bear families waiting for sea ice to form on Hudson Bay. Wapusk National Park, near Churchill, has one of the world's largest groups of polar bear maternity dens, where mothers give birth to cubs. Many of these dens were first dug by bears generations ago.

In this part of the Arctic, the sea ice melts completely in summer, usually in July. The bears mostly rest on land during the warm months. In the fall, they become more active and move to the coast. From early October, they gather along the shore of Hudson Bay. As soon as the ice is thick enough to hold them, they head out to hunt seals.

The cameras also help scientists. In December 2025, scientists confirmed that a wild mother polar bear had adopted a cub that was not her own. In spring 2025, she came out of her den with one tagged cub. By fall, she had two cubs, and only one had a tag. Cameras captured this rare behavior.

There is more to see. Viewers can ride along on the Tundra Buggy Lodge, a moving hotel made of linked vehicles, like a train. At night, a camera shows the northern lights dancing across the sky. Late winter and early spring are the best times to watch them.

Bird fans can also check out a raven cam, where ravens built a nest on top of an old observation tower.
why_it_matters: Livestreams let anyone watch wild animals and help scientists record rare behavior, like a polar bear adopting a cub.

background_read: Polar bears live in the Arctic and depend on sea ice as a platform for hunting seals, their main food.
Around Hudson Bay in Canada, the sea ice melts each summer, so the bears spend those months on land and return to the ice when the bay freezes again in late fall.
Scientists put tags on some bears so they can recognize them and follow their lives over time.
Wildlife cameras let scientists and the public watch animal behavior without disturbing the animals.
